hints: Focus on what each axis of a Boltzmann distribution must show, energy along the bottom and number of molecules up the side.
Notice that point X is a horizontal line across to the curve at $E_A$, so it reads off a single y-value at that energy.
Notice that point Y is the height of the top of the curve, so think about what the highest y-value means for number of molecules.
walkthrough:
**Recall the axes of the Boltzmann curve**

Remember this is a friendly distribution plot. The x-axis is molecular energy and the y-axis is number of molecules with that energy.

$$\text{x-axis} = \text{energy}, \quad \text{y-axis} = \text{number of molecules}$$

**Interpret point X at $E_A$**

Point X is on the vertical axis, level with the curve at $E_A$. So it is simply the y-value of the curve there, the number of molecules with energy exactly equal to $E_A$.

It is not the area to the right, the area beyond $E_A$ would be molecules with energy equal to or greater than $E_A$.

**Interpret point Y at the peak**

Point Y is on the vertical axis, level with the highest point of the curve. The peak is where the y-value is greatest, so it is the largest number of molecules sharing the same energy.

It is still a number on the y-axis, not an energy value on the x-axis. Putting X and Y together gives the correct pair.

options.A: Correct. Both X and Y are y-axis values, so both are numbers of molecules. X is the height of the curve at $E_A$, the number with energy equal to $E_A$. Y is the maximum height, the largest number of molecules with the same energy.
options.B: Incorrect for point X. The number with energy equal to or greater than $E_A$ is the whole area under the curve to the right of $E_A$, not the single y-value at $E_A$. This confuses a point height with an area.
options.C: Incorrect for point Y. The amount of energy of the greatest number of molecules is read from the x-axis below the peak (often called the most probable energy). Point Y is on the y-axis, so it must be a number of molecules, not an energy.
options.D: Incorrect for both. Point X confuses height with area beyond $E_A$, and point Y confuses a y-axis number with an x-axis energy. Remember both X and Y lie on the vertical axis, so both must be numbers of molecules.
